lesson.title: Theodore Roosevelt: The Accidental President Who Redefined the Office
lesson.summary: Theodore Roosevelt became president in September 1901 after the assassination of William McKinley, and over nearly eight years in office he turned the presidency into the driving force of the Progressive Era through trust-busting, conservation, consumer protection, and an assertive foreign policy.
lesson.body:
Theodore Roosevelt's path to the presidency ran through an unusually varied career: a sickly, asthmatic childhood he overcame through relentless physical exertion, a stint as a New York state assemblyman, several years ranching in the Dakota Territory, service as a federal Civil Service Commissioner and then as New York City's police commissioner, and a post as Assistant Secretary of the Navy. When the Spanish-American War broke out in 1898, Roosevelt resigned his Navy post to help lead a volunteer cavalry regiment known as the Rough Riders, gaining national fame for their charge up Kettle Hill near Santiago, Cuba. That fame helped propel him first to the governorship of New York and then, in 1900, onto the Republican ticket as President William McKinley's vice presidential running mate, a position some Republican bosses saw as a convenient way to sideline a reformer they found difficult to control.

That plan collapsed within months. McKinley was shot by an anarchist, Leon Czolgosz, at the Pan-American Exposition in Buffalo, New York, in September 1901, and died of his wounds on September 14. Roosevelt, at forty-two, became the youngest president in American history up to that time, taking office not through election but through assassination. He would go on to win a full term in his own right in the 1904 election.

Roosevelt used the presidency far more assertively than most of his predecessors, treating it as what he later called a bully pulpit for shaping public opinion and driving Congress toward action. His Square Deal domestic program combined regulation of corporations, consumer protections like the Pure Food and Drug Act, and an ambitious conservation agenda that set aside vast acreages of national forests and established the U.S. Forest Service, along with using the Antiquities Act of 1906 to protect sites like the Grand Canyon before Congress had acted. He pursued antitrust cases against corporate combinations, most famously the Northern Securities Company, in a campaign that came to be called trust-busting. Abroad, Roosevelt pursued an assertive foreign policy, beginning construction of the Panama Canal, sending the Great White Fleet on a world tour to display American naval power, and personally mediating an end to the Russo-Japanese War at the 1905 Treaty of Portsmouth, work for which he received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1906, the first American to win it.

Roosevelt left office in 1909 having hand-picked William Howard Taft as his successor, but he grew disillusioned with Taft's more cautious approach and challenged him for the Republican nomination in 1912. When party regulars backed Taft anyway, Roosevelt ran as the candidate of the new Progressive Party, nicknamed the Bull Moose Party, splitting the Republican vote and helping elect the Democrat Woodrow Wilson. Whatever one makes of that late chapter, Roosevelt's presidency had already permanently expanded what Americans expected the federal government, and the presidency itself, to do in response to the pressures of industrial society.
